Researchers found that blocked blood vessels in the brain accounted for much of the increase, while high blood pressure, diabetes, and substance use also became more common among younger stroke patients. Although survival rates have improved, more young adults may now face the lasting consequences of stroke.

items.title: [Fast Company] Half of the world’s population has been exposed to heat waves and wildfire smoke at the same time
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Climate change is a global phenomenon, meaning that everyone, in some way, will feel its devastating impacts. 

And increasingly, those impacts are happening simultaneously: Over the past two decades, more than half of the world’s population has experienced simultaneous heat waves and wildfires, occurring on the same day, a study found.

Researchers at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, published their findings this week in the journal Science Advances.

The study looked at 20 years of data, from 2000 to 2019. To see who experienced a wildfire, researchers looked at who was exposed to “fire-sourced air pollution”; their data took into account hourly temperature, fire emissions, air quality, and population information.

Over those 20 years, researchers found, the number of people around the world exposed to both wildfires and heat waves, on the same days, increased by 287 million—from 761 million people per year in the first half of that time period to more than 1 billion people per year in the second.

That means 55.9% of the global population has experienced at least one day where a heat wave and wildfire pollution occurred in tandem.

And the number of such days is increasing. From 2000 to 2009, the average person experienced one such day per year. Between 2010 and 2019, that rose to 1.7 days of co-exposure per person.

Damaging on multiple levels

The research doesn’t only illustrate how climate change is making extreme weather more frequent. It also shows how the health impacts of these events can compound as extreme weather overlaps.

Both heat waves and wildfires can cause serious harm to our health. Along with the risk of heatstroke—which can damage your brain, heart, and kidneys, and even be fatal—extreme heat and humidity can make it harder for some people to breathe, especially those with asthma or other lung conditions. 

Wildfires come with intense air pollution, full of tiny particles called PM2.5 (particulate matter 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter) that can get into our lungs and bloodstream, raising the risk of heart attack, stroke, and reduced lung function.

When heat waves combine with air pollution, the health impacts exacerbate. On days when an area sees a “double whammy” of high heat and high air pollution, the risk of death is three times greater “than the effect of either high heat or high air pollution alone,” health researchers have previously written. 

The Monash University researchers emphasize this in their study, too. “Compared with exposure to heat wave or landscape fire-sourced air pollution alone, co-exposure to both hazards may exert greater health impacts than the sum of their individual effects,” they write. 

In other words, the health risks—including respiratory and cardiovascular impacts—become amplified when wildfire air pollution and extreme heat happen together.

Extreme heat and wildfires also impact each event occurring. Conditions like high temperatures and dry soil promote wildfires, and wildfires then exacerbate heat waves because they release heat and pollution into the air.

“These processes create a positive feedback loop in which heat waves and fires amplify one another,” the researchers wrote.

Which regions are being hit hardest?

Some regions of the world are experiencing these simultaneous effects more than others. Zambia, for example, sees more than 28 such days per person every year. The Democratic Republic of the Congo comes in second, with just over 24 days per person per year.

Countries with lower life expectancy, education, and income tended to see the highest amount of wildfire and heat co-exposure, an example of the way that climate change is hitting the world’s poorest countries the hardest. 

Still, almost every area of the world saw an increase in this trend.

Central America, South America, Central and Eastern Africa, Southeast Asia, and parts of North America, Australia, and Russia all experienced “notable increases” in the annual average number of days that wildfire pollution and extreme heat occurred together.

items.title: [Fast Company] A timeline of New York City trying to ban horse carriages in Central Park
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The iconic but controversial horse-drawn carriage industry in New York City might finally come to an end as Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin reached a deal Tuesday to outlaw them.

If enacted, the bill would ban rides for hire starting June 1, 2028. 

Other NYC mayors have contributed to this effort, but none facilitated a full ban. Mamdani could be the first to achieve the full support of the City Council to effectively ban horse-drawn carriages.  

How prior mayors dealt with carriage controversies

When a horse collapsed from exhaustion in 2011, then-Mayor Michael Bloomberg dismissed a call to ban the industry, citing the importance of maintaining a livelihood of New York City’s carriage drivers.

In 2013, former Mayor Bill de Blasio was the first mayor to announce plans for a full ban. Without support from the City Council, however, the effort proved fruitless.

Just months before the end of his mayorship, de Blasio’s successor, Eric Adams, attempted to end horse-drawn carriage operations, which also lost due to a lack of support from the City Council. 

Why is Mamdani acting now?

An 18-year-old tourist from India, Romanch Mahajan, died after falling from a runaway carriage in July, which prompted “Romanch’s Law.”

The legislation will phase out the carriages while also providing a plan for protection of the workers whose livelihoods rely on the popular tourist activity. This time around, council members are expected to support the ban, after Menin publicly endorsed the law in July.

“The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected and the horses are safe,” Mamdani said in a statement on X on Tuesday. 

What’s at stake for the industry?

The industry salary is estimated at $65,000 to $70,000 per year, with approximately 68 active licenses and just under 160 horses licensed at the end of last year, according to the City Council’s Committee on Health.

As of May 3, 2025, the maximum fare for a carriage ride is $72.22 for the first 20 minutes, plus $28.89 for each additional 10 minutes. 

The 163-year-old industry brings tourism dollars into the city, although current estimates for just how much are hard to come by. (We’ve asked the NYC Horse & Carriage Alliance for more details.)

But it’s also yielded unsafe conditions for the horses and passengers. There have been 40 horse deaths between 1982 and 2026, the Manhattan borough president’s office found.

As the city moves toward a ban, the mayor is taking workers into consideration in the next stages.

CarriageOn, a coalition of carriage operators, cites itself as a diverse workforce, with immigrants at the forefront of its operation. There are questions about the future of these carriage operators, which the Mamdani administration aims to address.

The mayor’s office has been working on a detailed plan for the transition of the workforce and industry, a spokesperson on Mamdani’s team told Fast Company. 

Why does NYC have the horses in the first place?

Horse-drawn carriage rides for tourists date back to when Central Park opened in the 1800s, when carriages were already a mode of everyday transportation. Even then, people cited concerns about the horse-drawn vehicles. 

One of the most outspoken organizations is the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA), which was founded in New York City in 1866 amid a growing concern about the well-being of horses in the city.

Its original logo brandished an image of a carriage operator abusing a horse, while an angel hovered over the animal. Cruelty toward horses was a driving factor for the organization’s foundation, but horses also remained a vital part of transportation in the city. 

What would a ban mean for the horses?

As the tradition phases out, the horses need somewhere to go.

“If Romanch’s Law is enacted, the ASPCA stands ready to support the City through this transition,” ASPCA president and CEO Matt Bershadker told Fast Company. The organization is ready to provide “grant funding or other resources if necessary to help ensure humane placement and a safe future for every horse in need of a home,” he added.

Speaker Menin announced on Wednesday that the full council will vote on October 22 on the legislation.

“We have been working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all,” Sneha Choudhary, deputy press secretary for the mayor’s office, told Fast Company.

items.title: [Fast Company] Dementia cases are expected to more than double by 2050. A new study reveals who’s most at risk
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

More and more of our loved ones could develop dementia, as the number of diagnoses is projected to more than double by 2050, according to new research.

In the absence of large-scale prevention efforts, the number of people who are diagnosed with dementia each year could total 24.7 million by 2050, up from 11.4 million in 2023, according to a study by Australian researchers published in JAMA Neurology. Women and people who live in low- and middle-income countries already have higher rates of dementia, a trend that’s likely to continue, according to the findings.

While the researchers didn’t pinpoint an exact reason why dementia affects populations differently, they say the prospect of more cases warrants urgency in investing in prevention efforts. The prospect of 24 million new cases of dementia each year would place “enormous pressure on individuals, families, health systems and economies around the world,” Henry Brodaty, co-director of the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing at the University of New South Wales Sydney and a co-author of the study, said in a statement.

“We cannot simply wait for people to develop dementia and then respond,” Brodaty said. “We need to act across the spectrum—from reducing modifiable risk factors and identifying people at risk earlier, through to improving diagnosis, treatment and care.”

The researchers studied data from more than 38,000 people diagnosed with dementia spanning 18 countries or territories on six continents. They found that the incidence was somewhat higher among women—at 10.6 cases per 1,000 people versus 8.6 for men—but the difference was even starker depending on where people lived. The incidence of dementia was 13.6 cases per 1,000 people in low- and middle-income countries, compared with 8.3 in high-income countries.

Understanding the populations who are most at-risk for developing dementia will be key to developing prevention, diagnosis and care strategies, according to the study’s authors. 

“The higher incidence we observed in low- and middle-income countries is particularly concerning because these regions are experiencing rapid population aging while often having the fewest resources for prevention, diagnosis and care,” Perminder Sachdev, co-director of the Centre for Healthy Brain Ageing at the University of New South Wales in Sydney and a senior author of the study, said.

THE FINANCIAL TOLL OF DEMENTIA

Aging populations are understandably one of the main reasons why dementia cases are expected to increase, as this condition that affects memory, thinking and the ability to perform daily activities is more common after the age of 65. As of 2021, an estimated 57 million people worldwide were living with dementia, according to figures from the World Health Organization, and it’s the seventh leading cause of death.

The World Health Organization likewise estimated that as of 2019, dementia cost economies around the world about $1.3 trillion, so a surge in new cases also carries a financial toll. 

That’s why the new research should sound an alarm, as Dr. Liron Sinvani, director of research and innovation at the Northwell Institute for Healthy Aging and a professor at the Feinstein Institutes for Medical Research in New York, told U.S. News & World Report. “It’s an accelerating epidemic that demands immediate attention.” 

And that’s especially important as the countries that will face an “enormous wave” of dementia cases also have very limited infrastructure to respond, as Sinvani told the outlet. 

“Health systems must prepare for this massive increase in diagnostic and care demand, and this is especially true for these low- and middle-income countries where the growth will be fastest,” she said. “We know that dementia care requires a lot of caregiver support and is very costly. We will need a better infrastructure.”

items.title: [LoRaMeshDevices] Meshtastic Offline GPS Tracking: Save Your Route Without a Phone
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A Meshtastic device can send its GPS position over the air, but that is not the same as keeping a track on the device itself. In the standard setup I was using, disconnecting the phone meant the node continued broadcasting its location without saving a local history for later. I wanted something simple: take a node out for a walk, leave the phone disconnected, and download the route when I got home. So I modified the Meshtastic firmware to add on-device GPS location caching. I have this running on a SenseCAP T1000E and a Heltec T096. Both remain Meshtastic nodes, with their normal communication functions, but now they can also record a route independently of the phone. Key Takeaways The custom firmware records GPS points on the node without a connected phone. A 500-point cache provides roughly eight hours of recording at one point per minute. Reconnect to Meshtastic to load saved positions, then export them as GPX. Clearing app history does not clear the tracker cache; use the device controls to remove saved points. Table of ContentsWhat the Custom Tracker Firmware AddsUsing the Tracker Screen on the Heltec T096Button Controls on the SenseCAP T1000ESyncing Saved Tracks to the Meshtastic AppExporting Your Route as a GPX FileClearing the Tracker CacheInstalling the Firmware and Exploring the CodeWhat the Custom Tracker Firmware Adds Meshtastic is open source, and its module system gives you a useful way to add your own functionality without creating an entirely separate application. My modification adds a local cache for GPS points, controls for starting and stopping recording, and a way to replay those saved positions into the Meshtastic app. The basic workflow is: Start tracking on the device. Go walking or travelling without a connected phone. Reconnect to the Meshtastic app afterward. Let the saved positions populate the map. Export the track to GPX if you want to use it elsewhere. The device still sends position updates over the air as normal. Local recording is an additional function, not a replacement for Meshtastic communication. You can still receive messages and hear the usual notification sounds while recording your route. 500 points, recorded once per minute In this build, I set the cache capacity to 500 location points. With automatic recording every minute, that gives you roughly eight hours of tracking capacity, provided the device has a GPS location to save. That figure describes the number of points the cache can hold, not a battery-life measurement. You can also build up a collection of points across separate outings. One of my test devices had 205 points collected during experiments over about a month, while the other contained routes from several days of walking. Using the Tracker Screen on the Heltec T096 The T096 still has the familiar Meshtastic screens. I added one extra page for the tracker, showing whether recording is on or off and how many points are cached. For example, the display can show tracking switched off with 205 of 500 points cached. Stopping recording does not remove those points. They remain available to download later. To start recording: Navigate to the tracker screen. Long-press the button to open its menu. Select Start Tracking. Check that the tracker screen changes to Tracking On. With tracking enabled, the firmware saves a location every minute when a GPS position is available. The cached-point counter increases as points are recorded. A count of 205, for instance, becomes 206 after the next successful recording. To stop, open the menu again and select Stop Tracking. This stops the extra local recording function. The node continues doing its normal Meshtastic work, including sending positions according to its configuration. The same menu also includes Clear Cache, but save that until you have downloaded or exported anything you want to keep. Button Controls on the SenseCAP T1000E The T1000E does not have a screen, so I implemented the tracker controls through its button. The idea is to make it useful on its own, without needing to pull out a phone just to start a walk. Button action Tracker function One press Save the current location to the cache. Two presses Start or stop automatic recording every minute. Three presses Clear the cached locations. A double press starts recording with an audible beep. While recording, the device beeps every minute as it records. Double-press again to stop. The single-press action is handy when you just want to record where you are right now, rather than run continuous tracking. It writes that current location into the same cache. These shortcuts belong to this custom firmware. They are not instructions for the standard T1000E firmware. Syncing Saved Tracks to the Meshtastic App Once you return, connect to the device through the Meshtastic app as usual. There is no separate tracker app required for this part. Scan for nearby devices in the app's connection screen. Select the node you used for recording. Open that node's details and its Position history. Allow the connection to finish and the cached positions to arrive. The position history may initially look empty. In my demonstration, the connection indicator was orange while connecting, then turned green. Once connected, the saved positions started arriving and the route filled in on the map. The saved points populate the map after the node reconnects. On my T096, the downloaded history included driving routes as well as the walking route I use regularly. Connecting to the T1000E brought in its own saved points from several days of walking. Apparently, I do quite a lot of walking! Deleting app history does not clear the device This is an important distinction: the app's position history and the device's cache are separate. I deleted the position history in the app, disconnected, and connected again. The device replayed the saved positions, and the route appeared again. The points were still on the node. So, if a route returns after you delete it from the phone, that is expected. To remove the source of that replay, you need to clear the cache on the tracker itself. Exporting Your Route as a GPX File Once the positions are in the Meshtastic app, you can export them as a GPX file and open the result in another mapping application. I exported a test track, gave it a name, then opened it through the file browser in GPX Viewer. The same route appeared there, this time drawn over its map. The process is straightforward: Wait for the cached positions to finish loading into Meshtastic. Use the position-history export option to save a GPX file. Give the file a name. Open it in GPX Viewer or another application that supports GPX. I also included a Windows batch tool called tracker.bat. It provides another way to export a GPX file without using the Meshtastic app. The repository documentation explains that option. Clearing the Tracker Cache After saving your route, you can clear the device's cached positions so they no longer replay into the app. T1000E: Press the button three times. T096: Long-press to open the tracker menu, select Clear Cache, and confirm that you want to clear it. On the T096, the counter returns to 0 of 500. After I cleared the cache and reconnected, the old saved route no longer arrived. A current location could still appear, but that was a fresh position rather than the previous cached history. If you want to remove the route from both places, clear the app's history as well as the device's cache. Export anything important first. Installing the Firmware and Exploring the Code I put the firmware, source changes, and instructions in the tracker-firmware GitHub repository. It includes builds for the T096 and T1000E, device-control documentation, installation notes, and the Windows export tool. Before flashing, back up your Meshtastic configuration and export your keys. Do that first, before changing the firmware. For the demonstrated devices, installation uses the familiar flashing-mode and drag-and-drop process: Back up your existing configuration and keys. Download the firmware file that matches your device. Put the device into flashing mode. Drag and drop the matching firmware file onto the device's flashing drive. The flashing instructions shown for the T096 use two presses of Reset to make the drive appear. For the T1000E, hold the button while connecting the charging cable. Follow the repository's device-specific instructions rather than assuming that every Meshtastic board flashes the same way. How the modification fits into Meshtastic I used Meshtastic 2.8.1 for the demonstrated build. The tracker changes can also be incorporated into another firmware version and compiled, rather than being tied only to that build. The source changes are concentrated in four files. Part of the work changes the button-handling thread, because the tracker needs those additional button actions. The rest uses Meshtastic's optional add-on modules, which provide a place for custom functionality to run inside the firmware. I also compiled an ESP32-S3 version, mentioning Heltec V3 and V4 hardware as additional targets. That is separate from the hands-on T096 and T1000E examples here, so check the available files and instructions for your particular board. The LoRaWAN edition is a separate project I have a similar tracker project for the T1000E LoRaWAN edition, with comparable single-press and double-press controls. That project is aimed at LoRaWAN rather than Meshtastic. Do not confuse the LoRaWAN-edition firmware with the Meshtastic tracker build. There are supporting write-ups and architecture diagrams on the resource hub, but the firmware must match the device edition and the system you intend to use. What I like about this modification is how little it changes the everyday experience. It is still a Meshtastic node. It simply remembers where it has been, so you can take it out on its own and bring the route back afterward. Try the Offline GPS Tracker Firmware Get the T096 and T1000E firmware builds, source changes, installation instructions, and Windows GPX export tool. Get the Firmware on GitHub Frequently Asked Questions Does offline tracking stop the device from working as a Meshtastic node? No. The modification adds local location caching while retaining normal Meshtastic communication, including position broadcasts and message reception. Does the tracker save a point every minute without a GPS location? The automatic recording interval is one minute, but the device needs a GPS position available to save a location point. Why do deleted tracks return when I reconnect? Deleting position history in the app does not remove the points cached on the device. Reconnecting allows the node to replay them. Clear the device cache if you no longer want those saved positions to return. Can I export tracks without the Meshtastic phone app? Yes. The repository includes a Windows batch tool called tracker.bat that can export a GPX file without using the Meshtastic app.
